title: Vision: Zero Bugs — Johann Schleier-Smith, Temporal

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on agentic coding assurance and how formal methods can make AI-generated code achieve zero-bug reliability. The content targets software builders and developer platforms with coding-assistant reliability strategies. The discussion covers production-grade reliability and cost economics for deploying agentic coding systems. The talk assumes software engineering familiarity but explains formal methods at an accessible level. This is a conference-style talk with live demonstrations and structured argumentation. Twenty transcript-anchored evidence points with direct excerpts support the classification across all key themes.

The content targets software builders and developer platforms with coding-assistant reliability strategies. summary: Johann Schleier-Smith of Temporal Technologies presents a vision of software with literally zero bugs. He acknowledges practical, theoretical, and economic objections but argues aerospace examples—the Airbus A320, Space Shuttle, and Curiosity rover—prove near-perfect software is achievable through rigorous process, redundancy, specification-based design, and defensive programming. He traces seventy years of computer science advances: high-level languages (1950s–1980s) delivered 5–10x productivity gains; structured programming (Dijkstra, 1960s–1970s) replaced goto-driven flowcharts with compositional control structures; Parnas's modularity (1970s) enables subexponential or linear scaling of verification through local reasoning. These advances benefit LLM-generated code just as much as human-written code. He pitches Temporal's durable execution as abstracting away cloud reliability. The talk then covers formal methods, demonstrating Dafny's inline proofs with verification before execution, and cites commercial-scale successes: seL4, CompCert, Project Everest, and microprocessor design verification. Benchmark success rates rose from ~30% to nearly 100% while runtime dropped 50x over 20+ years. For agentic coding, he recommends detailed specifications, type languages, modular code, explicit risk analysis, safety cases, separate prompts for testing versus coding, multiple model providers, and formal proofs for critical sections. He introduces Software 3.0 (Karpathy)—programming through LLMs—where prompts function as programs, creating tremendous need for new assurance techniques because LLMs are non-deterministic with huge state spaces, though they also offer new resilience. On cost, he shows agentic coding is 1000–10000x cheaper than typical software development, while high-assurance code costs only ~100x more than typical software. Extrapolating, agents could produce high-assurance software 100x more cheaply than typical software is produced today, enabling a proliferation of bug-free experiences. He emphasizes this push addresses current agentic coding quality limitations, and once agents routinely produce fewer defects than human-written code, adoption will take off. He closes with Temporal's tardigrade mascot Ziggy, noting tardigrades' resilience—including survival in outer space—and invites collaboration.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Vision of Zero Bugs
sections.summary: Schleier-Smith introduces the vision of literally zero bugs, contrasting the everyday experience of non-engineers with the constant stress of software engineers. A mini golf reservation anecdote illustrates real-world bug impact.

sections.title: Objections to the Zero Bugs Vision
sections.summary: Three objection categories: practical (incidents happen, software is good enough), theoretical (code volume, specification ambiguity, unmodeled real-world events, verification intractability), and economic (competitor pressure, diminishing ROI, cynical support-revenue incentives).

sections.title: Aerospace Examples of Near-Zero-Bug Software
sections.summary: Airbus A320 achieved no software-attributed serious incidents via N-version programming, specification-based design, independent verification, defensive programming, static analysis, and zero-defect mindset. Space Shuttle reached ~1 error per 420,000 lines (~1000x better than typical commercial). Curiosity rover modernized the approach with identical redundancy and a commercial RTOS.

sections.title: Foundational Advances: High-Level Languages and Abstraction
sections.summary: High-level languages (1950s–1980s) replaced assembly and delivered a 5–10x productivity gain. Core ideas include data abstraction, structured programming, and the unifying principle of preserving essential complexity while removing implementation complexity.

sections.title: Structured Programming and Modularity
sections.summary: Structured programming (Dijkstra, 1960s–1970s) replaced goto-driven flowcharts with compositional control structures (sequences, selection, iteration), enabling hierarchical decomposition and mitigating complexity—equally valuable for LLM-generated code. Parnas's modularity (1970s) enables subexponential or linear scaling of verification through local reasoning at each level.

sections.title: LLMs, Libraries, and Temporal Pitch
sections.summary: LLMs benefit from high-level languages and libraries just as humans do: context is scarce, and properly testing and verifying generated library code is a huge challenge. Reliable, trusted components remain essential. Temporal provides durable execution, abstracting away cloud reliability into a separate codebase.

sections.title: Formal Methods and Dafny Demonstration
sections.summary: Dafny allows inline proofs with code, generating verified output in multiple languages. A live demo shows an array index search function verified before execution, with the verifier catching an introduced bug. Verification is only as good as the specification—omitted checks create bug opportunities.

sections.title: Commercial-Scale Formal Methods and Verification Tools
sections.summary: Formal methods successes include seL4 (fully verified OS), CompCert (verified C compiler), Project Everest (verified cryptography), and microprocessor design verification. Benchmark success rates rose from ~30% to nearly 100% while runtime dropped 50x. Tools span static verification (type systems), theorem proving (Dafny, F*, Spark, Lean), and model checking.

sections.title: Agentic Coding Strategies
sections.summary: Practical agentic coding strategies: detailed specifications, type languages, modular code, asking LLMs for explicit risk analysis and safety cases, separate prompts for testing versus coding, multiple model providers, formal proofs for critical sections, and keeping code small by outsourcing to libraries.

sections.title: Software 3.0 and New Assurance Challenges
sections.summary: Software 3.0 (Karpathy) treats prompts as programs. LLM non-determinism and huge state spaces make traditional verification inapplicable, creating a tremendous need for new assurance techniques. However, LLMs also offer new resilience, such as responding to unanticipated inputs.

sections.title: Agentic Coding Cost Economics
sections.summary: Schleier-Smith analyzes agentic coding costs with a vibe-coded game example: ~$2 using GPT5 Codeex, where output tokens are only ~15% of cost—the rest is input and reasoning tokens. He compares cost tiers: high-assurance code at $1,000–$3,000 per line (Space Shuttle, security software), typical software at $10–$100 per line, and low-cost contractors at $1–$10 per line. Agentic coding is 1000–10000x cheaper than typical software, while the gap between high-assurance and typical software is only ~100x, suggesting agents could produce high-assurance software 100x cheaper than typical software today.

sections.title: Vision of Zero Bugs and Closing
sections.summary: Software reliability is a solved problem in aerospace and critical industries. Agents equipped with formal methods, extensive processes, and adversarial testing can make high-assurance code 100x cheaper, enabling a proliferation of bug-free experiences. This push addresses current agentic coding quality limitations; once agents routinely produce fewer defects than humans, adoption will take off. Schleier-Smith closes with Temporal's tardigrade mascot Ziggy, noting tardigrades' resilience—including survival in outer space—and invites collaboration.
